text: Updates on my research and expository papers, discussion of open problems, and other maths-related topics. By Terence Tao 21 September, 2026 in advertising , math.GM | Tags: AI , Camilo De Lellis , Edward Witten , Francois Charles , Martin Hairer , Melanie Matchett Wood , Nikhil Srivastava , Ravi Vakil , Timothy Gowers , Ulrike Tillman | by Terence Tao [This is a guest post by the Advisory Group on Mathematics and Artificial Intelligence . This blog post was initially written in a different file format and converted using AI. — T.] We would like to use this guest post to announce the creation of the Advisory Group on Mathematics and Artificial Intelligence hosted at the Institute for Advanced Study (Princeton) and online at agmai.org . The rapid advances in artificial intelligence (AI) present both opportunities and challenges for mathematical research. We believe that we are at a historic moment for our discipline. Recent events raise urgent questions about how to support the long-term prospects for deep human understanding of mathematics. Purpose. The purpose of this group is to advise AI companies on their interactions with mathematical research and with the mathematical community, including the responsible presentation and release of mathematical results. We seek to work for the best interest of mathematics and the mathematical community, and to serve as one possible channel of communication between mathematicians and the AI industry. Independence, Transparency, and Accountability. This group operates independently of any AI company and members do not accept payment for this work. We will publish our recommendations to AI companies on this website. We are willing to offer such recommendations to any AI company whose models are likely to have a significant impact on mathematics. Although we will give advice, we do not have decision making power at any AI company, and the responsibility for the decisions made by any company will rest with that company. Advisory Group Members François Charles (ENS-PSL) Camillo De Lellis (IAS, GSSI) Timothy Gowers (College de France, Cambridge) Martin Hairer (EPFL, Imperial College London) Nikhil Srivastava (Berkeley, Simons Institute) Ulrike Tillmann (Oxford, INI) Ravi Vakil (Stanford) Edward Witten (IAS) Melanie Matchett Wood (Harvard) This group came together after OpenAI approached some of its members about establishing an external advisory board. In agreement with OpenAI, they decided to create an independent group and invite others to join. Current Task. We are currently facing the very specific challenge of advising OpenAI on how to coordinate the release of a large number of significant results in mathematics that they report have been produced by their internal model. We welcome input from the mathematical community on this question. Please use this form to share your thoughts with us as soon as possible . Your responses will be used to inform our recommendations and will not be made public without your approval. Is it a good idea to help their crisis management? 21 September, 2026 at 10:00 am just different What’s the alternative and why would it be better in the long run? 21 September, 2026 at 12:17 pm Michele Caselli At this point, I think some cooperation is better than no cooperation. I understand your concern about this being used as crisis management, but let’s be realistic here. There is already a widespread perception (from the way this buisness is reported in the media) that “math is solved” and that mathematicians are pushing to slow down AI mathematics so as not to lose their privilege/job. If we keep protecting our castle of glass and OpenAI publishes 100 open problems AI-solved tomorrow, without care for exposition or for the ideas being absorbed by the community as happened until now, I think the situation would become only worse. OpenAI does not need the mathematical community’s cooperation in order to publish results. It’s time some mathematicians step in, as an independent entity, to give some real and tangible guidance on what to do. Of course there is a risk that OpenAI benefits reputationally from this interaction, and this is a price to pay I guess, but pushing against any form of contact won’t fix the castle. The castle already has visible cracks, and letting this unfold without any cooperation would destroy it for sure. 21 September, 2026 at 9:56 am DH “This group of foxes has invited us to assist them in eating all the chickens as smoothly as possible. We invite suggestions from chickens on how best they can be eaten.” 21 September, 2026 at 9:56 am Anonymous Hello! I am a second year PhD student in pure mathematics, and the phrase “…a large number of significant results in mathematics that they report have been produced by their internal model.” really disheartens me. Especially without saying how many results and what results. I understand that such advancement are important for mathematics, but my little human brain can’t help but interpret that my time spent on my PhD is going to be a waste of time. Spending 4 years on something that an agent swarm could prove in 1 day, or less. Forgive my pessimism. I’ve seen a lot of mathematicians talking about the current situation with varying degrees of enthusiasm, ranging from complete rejection of LLMs to unquestionable assimilation in the community. I believe there’s a lot to be gained by computer assisted maths, but personally, I’m not sure this would be a profession in which I would like to take part in. Vibe-prompting LLMs for answers. But, for better or for worse, future does not follow a set list of rules. I guess only time will tell how things evolve… I might be giving the impression of a shallow person, and I might as well be one, but the current state of affairs feels overwhelming to me. I believe this is a reasonable reaction for my career stage, and of course part of human nature. But human nature can easily be decieved. To my mind comes the following paraphrase from Thucydides: “People always think the greatest war is the one they are fighting at the moment, and when that is over they are more impressed with wars of antiquity” Maybe everything will turn out to be alright and we’re just in the middle of a proverbial panic attack. But wishful thinking is not enough. Action needs to be taken to preserve what is worth preserving in the community and to amend what can not withstand the future.
